The Śrī Yogaprakaraṇa: A Commentary on the Sarvajñānottara.
Hereafter, I shall explain Yoga.
Because yoga is the means for exhausting the impurities and so forth projected by the effects initiated [by past karma], it has a connection with the categories of existence (*padārtha*);

this is a "chapter-wise" (*pāṭalika*) connection, as yoga constitutes the subject matter of the chapter. Because it possesses two causes, the connection with the context (*prakaraṇa*) is indicated by the word "pure" (*śuci*), and the connection with the aphorism (*sūtra*) is established through its being part of the section on yoga.

Or rather, by means of the very word "compendium" (*samuccaya*), the yogi who consists of the sentence [attains] the qualities that consist of yoga through various sentences. Therefore, immediately after the section on conduct (*caryākāṇḍa*), I shall explain yoga concisely and with excellence. To whom does this purification of yoga belong? To this he says:

But for one who is solitary, peaceful, self-controlled, dispassionate, and free from longing; for one whose food and movement are prescribed, whose actions are prescribed, and whose sleep and waking are prescribed—
listen truly, O Six-faced One, to how this [discipline] is a purifier for such a person alone, and not for anyone else.

The meaning is "of the mind, like [the stillness] of waters. Because of the Śiva-yoga which reveals omniscience and other such qualities— [yoga] belonging to one who is solitary, who possesses no belongings due to the renunciation of all attachments,
who is in the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and who is peaceful, being free from violence and the like.

The meaning is: "of one who is endowed with *yama* and *niyama*. For *yama* is the restraint of the mind, and *niyama* is the restraint of the senses. As Patañjali said: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*."
Purity, contentment, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas).

Therefore, for one whose mind is restrained, who has been brought under control through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and who is characterized as omniscient by virtue of the power of [his] feet; for such a dispassionate person, endowed with world-weariness (*vairāgya*), free from longing, and averse to worldly enjoyments—(p. 2)—[he becomes a knower].
"For one who is disciplined in diet and conduct, that [state] which is like the king of beasts... and so forth, including "one who is healthy from eating what is digested.
Furthermore, for one who is disciplined in exertion in all actions—that is, performing what is appropriate—and who observes the stated times for sleep and waking, his yoga should be meditated upon.

Therefore, listen to that which consists of the relationship with the meditator (*dhyātṛ*). It is not, however, of the nature of *samādhi* as it is heard [in other systems] as a limb of yoga, such as that of Patañjali and others; as it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), meditation (*dhyāna*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*)."
"Discipline, concentration, and likewise meditative absorption—this is called the six-limbed yoga."

For this very reason, the word *yoga* is derived from the root *yuj* in the sense of "joining" (*yoga eva*), and not from *yuj* in the sense of "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*). Indicating precisely this, he states that only the man of knowledge possesses the qualification for yoga:
"That which is to be meditated upon, that by which one meditates, and that which is the purpose of meditation—all these, he who [unites], that is yoga."
It ought to be performed; and by the word "ca" (and), it is meant that it is also the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). As it has been said:
"The self is the meditator, the mind is the meditation, and the subtle Maheśvara is the object of meditation.
That which is the supreme sovereignty—this is the purpose of meditation, [and] the mind [is the instrument]."
The meaning is that reflection (*cintā*) is the contemplation of the true nature of the object as it is. From that, meditation (*dhyāna*) is described;

meditation is the contemplation of the form of that which has been heard. Now, one might object that "mind" (*manas*) and "consciousness" (*citta*) are synonymous, [but] this is not so, because it is not established as a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*). Furthermore, this is merely an illustration; other [limbs] are also [included].
Having understood the limbs of sacrifice (*yāga*), the limbs of the self (*aṅgin*), and yoga, one should practice yoga.
Furthermore:
having made honor and dishonor equal, and likewise pleasure and pain equal.
Having completely abandoned joy, fear, and despondency, one should practice yoga.
As they say:
"He who does not rejoice at a benefit nor become angry at an injury,
who is equal toward all beings— he is considered one who has lived as a liberated soul."
Now, the section on the stages of yoga: In an empty house, a delightful monastery, or an auspicious temple;
or on a secluded riverbank, or even in a formidable forest.
In a place that is secluded, solitary, and free from people;
liberated from the defects of yoga, free from conceptual construction, and without glare.
The defects of yoga are ants and the like. "Non-conceptual" means being free from conceptual constructions such as "belonging to another" and so forth.
The commencement of the practice of yoga:
Having bathed, become pure, and sipped water for purification, and having bowed his head to Śiva and paid homage to the teacher of yoga, a person should apply himself to yoga.
He describes the yogic postures: "Either the lotus (padma) or the svastika, as well as the añjali;
for the sake of a seat, either the half-moon (ardhacandra) or the sarvatobhadra."
Having assumed a comfortable posture characterized by the lotus-posture (*padmāsana*) and others,
as described in other *saṃhitās*.
Now he states the method of practice: (p.
4) With the upper body erect and the head level, having abandoned all attachments, with the cave of the mind established in the Self.
The word "should do" (*kuryāt*) is to be supplied [from the previous verse].
Therefore, having abandoned all attachments, one should make the mind abide in the Self;
that is, one should perform the withdrawal (*pratyāharaṇa*) of the mind—the presiding authority over all the senses—from its objects.

Thus, by this, the limb of yoga called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) should be understood in brief. Furthermore, at that time, one should not let the teeth touch the teeth, nor the corners of the mouth with the tongue; rather, with the eyes slightly contracted, one should properly utter the syllable *Śiva*. This is the time for *pratyāhāra*.
The meaning is that one should mentally recollect the root which consists of the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Now, as for the purpose of its utterance:
it causes the principles (*tattva*) beginning with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) to ascend from embodied beings. This is the intended meaning; [it is] Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Due to the elision of the *visarjanīya*, the Śiva-mantra is as will be described hereafter. Preceded by a *sagarbha-prāṇāyāma*, when this [mantra] is uttered while being presided over by Śiva, it reveals the *tattvas* through the sequence of attaining *samādhi*. *Manas*.
Through the continuous connection [with the Guru], there arises the union with the desired state presided over by Śiva; that is to say, the direct realization of each respective [principle] occurs.

As for "tanmātra" and so forth, those which are the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as earth and the rest, and those which are the primary [elements], all these principles (*tattva*) belong to these senses and so on.
It should be understood that [the scripture] illuminates [these matters] as stated in the *Śrīmanmataṅga* and other texts. And those are the principles (*tattva*).
Furthermore, he says that through the contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of that very scripture, one turns away from bondage:
"And again, the six-faced one (*Ṣaḍānana*), being unattached, is the destroyer. The word "of them" (*teṣām*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

At that time, since the ancillary parts (*aṅga*) also arise from that [same source], he states that they do not require separate recitation: "His heart, head, crest-lock, armor, weapon, and eyes—along with them—all proceed from that very [source] alone. Now, let us consider the state of *prāṇāyāma* with seed-syllables (*sagarbha*).
He states that meditation should be performed preceded by the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) of retention (kuṃbhaka):
"Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the suṣumnā,
and having restrained their activity, the wise man should meditate on Śiva, the Self."
The nature of *sagarbha* (with seed) breath control is also stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"That [breath control] is 'with seed' when accompanied by meditation and recitation; it is 'discarded' when the [seed-mantra] has been set aside."
Now, he describes the state of culmination of that very meditation:

"The wise one always [perceives] that which is conjoined with inseparable connection, whose form is light, perfectly pure, extremely subtle, all-pervading, eternal, and free from conceptual construction."
"Non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*) means that, through the manifestation of the form of the object of meditation, one is free from the [distinctions of] the meditator and so forth.
As Patañjali said: "Dhyāna is the extension of the cognitive state (*pratyaya*);
that same [state], when devoid of its own [subjective] form, is samādhi. Thus, there is a distinction between the "pregnant" (*sagarbha*) and the "wombless" (*nigarbha*).
Having stated the twofold nature of the breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), he now describes their threefold nature:

"The sagarbha [breaths] are remembered as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and slow. The term "sagarbha" is an elliptical expression; for immediately thereafter, the classification of the *agarbha* [breaths] into superior and so forth is also mentioned.
He will say: "Furthermore, he states the threefold nature [of breath control]:

'One should perform those breath controls (prāṇāyāmas), namely inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). Regarding the breath controls and so forth that possess the 'seed' (sagarbha), it has been stated that through the sequence of attaining meditative absorption (samādhi), there is mastery over the principles (tattva)."
(p. 6) He states the fruit for those who are without the *garbha*:
"By means of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one removes external defects; by means of concentrations (*dhāraṇā*), one removes sin;
by means of withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), one destroys [the effects of] past actions; and by means of meditation (*dhyāna*), one destroys imperishable qualities."

The meaning is that qualities such as [lightness] arise as long as the body exists. It is established that the body becomes non-perishable (*anaśvara*), not empty (*aśūnya*), and even attains stability. Now, he states the definition of *pūraka* and the other [breath-controls]: "Having filled the abdomen with air for as long as desired..."
Prāṇāyāma indeed consists of the pūraka, which fills the body;
having closed all the openings and being devoid of inhalation and exhalation,
one should remain like a completely filled jar— that is kumbhaka prāṇāyāma.
Then one should exhale the breath accompanied by gentle exhalation;
this is known as *recaka*, which can cause danger to life.
It is stated that *pūraka* and *recaka* should be performed through the left and right channels (*nāḍī*) respectively.

"He causes the risk of life" is said because, at the time of departure [from the body], the exhalation (*recaka*)— preceded by the severing of the knots— is the cause of the separation from the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
He states the distinction between the "superior" and other types based on the difference in the timing of these very [exhalations].
Having extended the right hand and placed the knee [on the ground], one should perform a circumambulation from left to right.
One should then give a snap of the fingers; this is called a *mātrā*.
Twelve *mātrās* are to be known as the measure termed a *tāla*, and twelve *tālas* are to be known as a *prāṇāyāma*. What is its [the breath's] nature?
The middle one, however, is twenty-four, while the eldest should be double that.
And the rule for their practice is as follows: (p.
7) The best of those who know yoga should increase the measure by one each day;
he should increase it only in a gradual sequence, whether quickly or slowly.
Now, he states the duration for concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and so forth, regarding the mind fixed upon the nature of the object of meditation in locations such as the heart:
"That which is the supreme *prāṇāyāma*, twice that is considered *dhāraṇā*."
Yoga is twice as effective as dhāraṇā, and yoga itself is doubled;
this is known as the perfection of yoga (yogasiddhi) by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
In this context, by the word *yoga*, even the contemplation of the true nature of the object of meditation is intended;
it is called *adhyāna* (meditative absorption) because it constitutes a connection between the meditator and that which is meditated upon.
By the term *yogasiddhi*, however, *samādhi* (concentration) is meant. [This refers to] the stages of *dhāraṇā*, *adhyāna*, and *samādhi*.
Because they are heard of as being attained in sequence through the limbs of yoga.
Now, an objection: in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, an increase in duration for *dhāraṇā* and the subsequent stages is heard;
for it is said there:
This time, characterized by the quality of the sun (arka-guṇa), attains the state known as *dhāraṇā* when the mind is firmly established;
it is called *dhāraṇā* because it bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Twelve *dhāraṇās* constitute meditation (*dhyāna*) through the manifestation of divine light;
these twelve are the cause for the attainment of *samādhi*, the *maṇi* [power], and the other [siddhis].

It is true that there is no contradiction because the division of ritual action (*kriyā*) is the cause for the division of the Tantras; however, Yoga—which consists of the direct realization of the object to be meditated upon—is a specific connection (*viśeṣasaṃbandha*). Thus he says: "Then one perceives within oneself the subtle *gandhatanmātra*."
One perceives taste, heat, touch, and the subtle element of sound itself,
in successive order, through various states of color.
One should understand egoism, mind, intellect, the qualities, the unmanifest, and the Puruṣa; as well as the manifested [elements], characterized by their own specific properties and qualities.
Then, having seen Vidyā, Kalā, Kāla, and Māyā, and then Vidyā once more, he should pierce them all in due order with the Astra-mantra.
Then, having abandoned the principle of Vidyeśvara and thereafter the supreme Sādāśiva with the weapon of the razor-knife (kṣurikāstra), one should enter the subtle Śiva, bypassing the Sun (arka).
And here, since gross elements can be known even through direct perception, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth are said to be realizable solely through yogic intuition;
for even the true nature of earth and the other elements [is realized] through subtle yoga.
It is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures that [the reality] must be directly realized (*sākṣātkartavya*).
Therefore, having thus directly realized the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva,
one should pierce and conquer them with the *kṣūrikā-astra* joined with the Root-mantra (*mūlayukta*), as previously described.

The meaning is that one should cause [the soul] to turn back from bondage. For it was stated previously: "He causes the principles (tattvas) beginning with the subtle elements (tanmātras) of embodied beings to rise up; and he who is joined with the weapon is the destroyer once again, O Six-faced One.
Thus, by means of yoga with a support (sālambana-yoga), one should unite one's own self with the partless Śiva; this is the meaning.

And here, because it is useful for the conquest of reality (*tattvajaya*), even that limb of yoga called reasoning (*tarka*) mentioned in other treatises is indeed established by implication, as it is heard: "Reasoning is an internal factor of yoga.
Now, he demonstrates the fruit of yoga.
Śiva, whose nature is nectar, is directly present within that [yogi] who knows yoga;
he becomes omniscient, omnipresent, subtle, the Lord of all, and the creator of all.
Now, one might object: if liberation is accomplished through yoga alone, does it not follow that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is likewise useless?

Therefore, since such Śiva-yoga cannot be accomplished without initiation (dīkṣā), and because its purpose is fulfilled solely by the removal of impurities (mala) and so forth projected by karma whose effects have already begun, [the Śiva-scripture is not for] those who lack qualification [to receive it]. Without the Śiva-scripture...

Furthermore, because of the absence of knowledge and so forth regarding the totality of principles (*tattva*), and precisely to avoid the consequence of [the term] being merely [a negation], he shows the object to be known (*jñeya-vastu*). In all the scriptures, the object to be known consists of fourfold entities.

The bound soul (*paśu*), the bond (*pāśa*), and the Lord (*pati*)—these are Śiva himself in their respective order. Here, the Lord (*pati*) is Śiva himself in the state of exercising authority; therefore, he is the referent of the term *pati*. We shall explain that this very [Lord], when possessed of limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*) and when free from them (*nirupādhika*), is spoken of figuratively as two distinct types.
And thus, since knowledge is also a constituent part of initiation and so forth, its status as a cause of liberation is established by way of a traditional succession; he says:
"But having known the true nature of reality, which is the essence therein and difficult to attain..."
Even while revolving in every way, he does not again take up a body.
Thus ends the chapter on Yoga in the commentary on the Śrī-Sarvajñānottara, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, the teacher of two hundred thousand [verses].
